title: Opinion and principle
hookLine: the Hanafi method uses reasoned opinion and juristic preference

lines: A FASTING MAN FORGETS AND DRINKS.
cards: A fasting man forgets. It's the middle of a long day, there's water on the table, and he drinks before he remembers. Has he broken his fast?
Follow a straight line of logic and the answer is yes: the fast means no drink, and he drank.
But in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says whoever forgets while fasting and eats or drinks should complete the fast, because it was Allah who fed him and gave him drink.

A story told about Abu Hanifa has him say that if it weren't for that report, he would have followed the logic. What do you call setting the obvious rule aside for a stronger reason? Today has two words for it.

teach.b: The first is ra'y, opinion, but not the kind you shout across a dinner table. In law it means a considered judgment, reached by a trained mind where no text settles the question.

In Kufa, Abu Hanifa and his circle used it so carefully, and so often, that critics called them the people of ra'y. Some meant it as a warning; the Hanafis took it as a description of hard work. And it keeps an order.

teach.h: THE BOOK, THE SUNNAH, THEN THE MIND.
teach.b: A saying attributed to Abu Hanifa lays it out: the Book of Allah first, then the sunnah of the Prophet, then the sayings of the companions. Only after that did his own judgment begin.
The second word is istihsan, juristic preference, often explained as counting one answer the better one.
Sometimes a plain analogy points one way and a stronger reason points another: a report, a real hardship, the settled practice of people.
Istihsan chooses the stronger reason, and the forgetful faster is a case Hanafi books give for it. Not everyone agreed.
Al-Shafi'i, whom you'll meet soon on this path, wrote that preference without a text is a jurist pleasing himself.
Hanafi scholars answered that istihsan is never a mood: it's a preference with a proof behind it, named and open to challenge.
The two schools still disagree about the word, and both say the texts come first.

how: Hanafi jurists reach rulings from the Qur'an and sunnah first, then use considered judgment and juristic preference, choosing a stronger proof over a plain analogy, in questions the texts leave open.

o: a jurist's personal whim, chosen by taste or mood
a considered judgment where no text settles the question
a ruling that every scholar has already agreed on

games.q: opinion and principle — tap the pairs.
p: warned against preference without a text

s: ra'y means a jurist's personal whim
it means a considered judgment, used where no text settles the question, after the Qur'an and sunnah.
critics called the jurists of Kufa the people of ra'y
some meant it as a warning; the Hanafis took it as a description of hard work.
the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools agree about istihsan
al-Shafi'i criticized it; Hanafi scholars defend it as a preference with a proof behind it.

games.q: a fasting man forgets and drinks water at midday. what does the report in Sahih al-Bukhari tell him?
o: his fast is broken; make it up later.
complete the fast: Allah fed him and gave him drink.
fast an extra day as a penalty.
games.why: he completes the fast. the straight line of logic said broken; the report says otherwise, and the jurists follow the report.

practice: Pick a small decision where both answers are decent: call your mother tonight or visit this weekend, finish the work or rest.

Hold each side and name its reason plainly, the obvious rule on one side and any stronger reason on the other, someone's need, a promise, a cost you hadn't counted, as if you had to explain it to a fair friend.
If you pray, you can ask for good judgment.

wordCard.voice: Ra'y. Opinion: in law, a considered judgment where no text settles the question; with istihsan, choosing the stronger reason. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: opinion, view, considered judgment; in law, reasoning where no text settles the question.

carryVoice: Your line: reasoned preference. A preference with a proof behind it is never just a mood. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1933 (whoever forgets while fasting and eats or drinks, let him complete his fast)
